sources.title: Swarm Intelligence — Dorigo & Birattari, Scholarpedia
sources.why_use: Canonical narrow definition; local interaction, self-organization, ACO and PSO.
sources.limits: Foundational taxonomy, not an LLM or social-media deployment study.

quotes.text: The characterizing property of a swarm intelligence system is its ability to act in a coordinated way without the presence of a coordinator or of an external controller.

sources.title: Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey of LLMs — Tran et al.
sources.why_use: Taxonomy of LLM multi-agent architecture; supports separating orchestration from decentralized swarm behavior.
sources.limits: Broad survey, not independent replication of all surveyed claims; v1 is deliberately pinned.

quotes.text: Our framework characterizes collaboration mechanisms based on key dimensions: actors (agents involved), types (e.g., cooperation, competition, or coopetition), structures (e.g., peer-to-peer, centralized, or distributed), strategies (e.g., role-based or model-based), and coordination protocols.

sources.title: How malicious AI swarms can threaten democracy — Schroeder et al.
sources.type: Science Policy Forum; author accepted version v4
sources.why_use: Specific online malicious-swarm capability definition and proposed policy/technical defenses.
sources.limits: Threat analysis and proposals, not a demonstrated autonomous online swarm; published examples must be independently checked.

quotes.text: Local adaptation plus periodic synchronization with a central node blurs the line between command-and-control and emergent “hive” behavior.

sources.title: Stigmergy as a universal coordination mechanism I: Definition and components — Heylighen
sources.why_use: Defines indirect action-trace-action coordination and explains why direct messages are not necessary.
sources.limits: General coordination theory; does not establish machine authorship or malicious intent.

quotes.text: The present paper clarifies the issue by defining stigmergy as a mechanism of indirect coordination in which the trace left by an action in a medium stimulates subsequent actions.

sources.title: Is this the real life? Is this just fantasy? The Misleading Success of Simulating Social Interactions With LLMs — Zhou et al.
sources.why_use: Shows why omniscient dialogue simulation is not equivalent to real multi-agent social behavior.
sources.limits: Specific models and tasks; does not prove all later social-agent systems fail.

quotes.text:
Our findings indicate that addressing
information asymmetry remains a fundamental
challenge for LLM-based agents.

sources.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? — Cemri et al.
sources.type: Empirical research paper; pinned arXiv v3
sources.why_use: Empirical failure taxonomy and trace dataset; counterweight to automatic collective-intelligence claims.
sources.limits: Selected frameworks/benchmarks and partly LLM-annotated traces; failure rates are not universal swarm rates.

quotes.text: This process identifies 14 unique modes, clustered into 3 categories: (i) system design issues, (ii) inter-agent misalignment, and (iii) task verification.

sources.title: Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet
sources.type: academic preprint, full text (arXiv v1; later journal reference shown in arXiv metadata)
sources.why_use: Empirical 1,140-account botnet; explicit separation of current rule-based automation from hypothetical fully autonomous agents; network and detector evaluation.
sources.limits: Single Twitter botnet; inference of ChatGPT from refusal messages, not provider logs; not all content known to be AI-generated; no measured external persuasion. Web-extracted chart tables contain implausible reconstructed values and are not used; native pdftotext prose is preferred.

quotes.text:
The fox8 bots currently operate under some pre-established rules and only use
ChatGPT for content generation and dialogues.

sources.title: "Bad Grammar": Russian-linked Telegram comment activity
sources.why_use: Clear human-operated AI-assisted commenting pipeline; at least a dozen Telegram accounts; explicit low-impact assessment.
sources.limits: Provider-held prompt and account data not publicly reproducible; no exact total post/account count or formal attribution confidence; visible engagement cannot measure all exposure.
sources.date_provenance: Originally in May 2024 report announced May 30 (OPENAI-MAY); reprint page displays May 1, 2024, which is not used as original publication day.

quotes.text: The network used our models and accounts on Telegram to set up a comment-spamming pipeline. First, the operators used our models to debug code that was apparently designed to automate posting on Telegram. They then generated comments in Russian and English in reply to specific Telegram posts. Finally, they appear to have used at least a dozen Telegram accounts to post those comments.

sources.title: Operation "Doppelganger": Russian influence activity targeting Ukraine
sources.why_use: Functional specialization, AI-to-published-content matching, and documented artificial reply/amplification patterns, rather than proof of decentralized agents.
sources.limits: Four clusters are provider-side account groups, not four independent networks or a social-account total; reach assessment is only the AI-associated slice; attribution authority chain is cited by OpenAI, not independently audited here.
sources.date_provenance: Originally in May 2024 report announced May 30 (OPENAI-MAY); reprint displays May 1.

quotes.text: We banned four clusters of accounts using our models linked to people acting on behalf of the Russian influence operation known as [“Doppelganger”⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.disinfo.eu/doppelganger-operation/). Each cluster displayed different tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), consistent with an operation made up of different functional teams.

sources.title: Operation "Spamouflage": China-linked influence activity
sources.why_use: Directly observed AI use inside an older coordinated influence/harassment network; makes the AI-versus-total-output distinction explicit.
sources.limits: Small unspecified number of OpenAI accounts; does not establish AI use across the full Spamouflage network. Do not double-count alongside Graphika Wolf News or U.S.-persona reports. External Meta/FBI attribution is reported by OpenAI and not independently verified in this bundle.
sources.date_provenance: Originally in May 2024 report announced May 30 (OPENAI-MAY); reprint displays May 1.

quotes.text: The network’s use of artificial intelligence appears to have constituted only a minority of its overall output.

sources.title: Operation "Zero Zeno": Israel-linked influence activity
sources.why_use: Commercial campaign operator, synthetic personas, recycled images, self-replies, cross-platform distribution, and explicit deletion-related measurement caveat.
sources.limits: STOIC is the operator attributed by OpenAI, not itself the campaign name or a verified commissioning state; no total public account count; deleted accounts limit historical engagement visibility; profile-face generation is an assessment, not proof of image-tool source.
sources.date_provenance: Originally in May 2024 report announced May 30 (OPENAI-MAY); reprint displays May 1.

quotes.text: Zero Zeno’s activity appears to have attracted little if any engagement, other than from its own inauthentic accounts. (Many accounts have already been disabled by Meta and X, so current engagement figures may not present the complete picture.)

sources.title: Disrupting a covert Iranian influence operation
sources.why_use: Exact public-asset counts with explicit units; two human-operated content workstreams; investigation seeded by published Microsoft reporting; little demonstrated organic traction.
sources.limits: Count is an observed subset as of August 2024, not provider-account count or full network; Iranian attribution relies in part on Microsoft reporting; publication-to-model matching does not reveal agent control architecture or total web readership.

quotes.text: Our investigation revealed that this operation used ChatGPT for two purposes: generating long-form articles and shorter social media comments. The first workstream produced articles on U.S. politics and global events, published on five websites that posed as both progressive and conservative news outlets. The second workstream created short comments in English and Spanish, which were posted on social media. We identified a dozen accounts on X and one on Instagram involved in this operation.

sources.title: Disrupting deceptive uses of AI by covert influence operations
sources.type: primary provider synthesis of five influence-operation disruptions
sources.why_use: Defines assessed campaign subset and period; AI adoption/productivity/defender-tooling observations; provides original-report publication date for reprinted case studies.
sources.limits: Overlaps the four case reprints and IUVM, so not an additional network or independent corroboration; provider selection/visibility and disrupted-case survivorship biases; impact assessment does not measure causal attitude change.

quotes.text: **Mixing old and new**: All of these operations used AI to some degree, but none used it exclusively. Instead, AI-generated material was just one of many types of content they posted, alongside more traditional formats, such as manually written texts or memes copied from across the internet.

sources.title: Deepfake It Till You Make It: Pro-Chinese Actors Promote AI-Generated Video Footage of Fictitious People in Online Influence Operation
sources.type: primary independent threat-intelligence report, full PDF
sources.why_use: Synthetic-video provenance from reused commercial avatars; two unique content artifacts, not a bot-account total; provides documented reverse-image-search/catalog matching and <=300-view outcome.
sources.limits: Part of Spamouflage, not a separate swarm. Strong assessment of Synthesia use, but no provider logs disclosed, and no proof the scripts were LLM-generated. Full public PDF recovered despite a now-gated landing page.
sources.date_provenance: graphika-deepfake.md landing publication date; full PDF says 02.2023

quotes.text:
This set of two unique videos shared many of the same characteristics as traditional
Spamouflage content: they ranged between one-and-a-half and three minutes in length, used a
compilation of stock images and news footage from online sources, and were accompanied by
robotic English-language voiceovers promoting the interests of the Chinese Communist Party.

sources.title: The #Americans: Chinese State-Linked Influence Operation Spamouflage Masquerades as U.S. Voters to Push Divisive Online Narratives Ahead of 2024 Election
sources.type: primary independent threat-intelligence report, full PDF
sources.why_use: Older network adapting U.S. voter personas; corroborating coordination indicators, high-confidence attribution, and a substantial view-count exception to typical low traction.
sources.limits: 15 X accounts and one TikTok account plus a cross-platform media persona are a studied subset, not whole-network scale; counts should not be added without identity deduplication. Viral video is not established as AI-generated or as causing opinion change. OCR ligature spacing remains in saved body and exact quote.
sources.date_provenance: graphika-americans-metadata.md landing publication date; PDF metadata modification date agrees

quotes.text:
The Harlan Report TikTok account garnered signifi cant views for several videos,
including one pinned video mocking Biden with 1.5 million views.

sources.title: Uncovering Coordinated Networks on Social Media: Methods and Case Studies
sources.status: Evaluated research framework, not verified as platform production
sources.why_use: General account–feature bipartite graph projection; exact distinction coordination vs intent/automation.
sources.limits: Five Twitter case studies; manual tuning/validation; chance-graph null model is future work, not evaluated.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
Our approach aims to identify coordination between accounts, but it does not characterize the intent or authenticity
of the coordination, nor does it allow to discover the underlying mechanisms. An example of malicious intent was
highlighted in recent news reports about a coordinated network of teenagers posting false narratives about the election.<sup>6</sup> However, it is important to keep in mind that coordinated campaigns may be carried out by authentic users
with benign intent. For instance, social movement participants use hashtags in a coordinated fashion to raise awareness of their cause.

More rigorous methods could be investigated to exclude
spurious links that can be attributed to chance. One approach
we plan to explore in future work is to design null models
for the observed behaviors, which in turn would enable a formal statistical test to identify meaningful coordination links.
For example, one could apply Monte Carlo shuffling of the
bipartite network before projection to calculate the *p*-values
associated with each similarity link.

Although the proposed
method is unsupervised and therefore does not required labeled training data, we recommend a manual inspection of
the suspicious clusters and their content. Such analysis will
provide validation of the method and evidence of whether
the coordinated groups are malicious and/or automated.

sources.title: Coordinated Behavior on Social Media in 2019 UK General Election
sources.status: Implemented and evaluated research; no production claim
sources.why_use: Rare co-retweet weighting, multiscale backbone, iterative Louvain and continuous coordination index.
sources.limits: Top active-user selection, single political event, coordination/authenticity distinction remains unresolved.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
The TF-IDF weight allows us to reduce the relevance of
highly popular tweets in our dataset and emphasize similarities due to retweets of unpopular tweets – a much more
suspicious behavior.

Despite still not distinguishing inauthentic coordinated
behaviors from authentic ones, our work makes a step forward in this direction by providing more nuanced and more
accurate results.

We begin by performing community detection on the filtered network resulting from
step 4, identifying the set *C<sub>0</sub>* of communities. Then, we
apply an increasingly restrictive similarity threshold t<sub>i</sub>
to edge weights at each iteration, thus removing certain
edges and disconnected nodes. We repeat community detection on the obtained subnetwork G<sup>e,v</sup><sub>i</sub>. At each iteration, the community detection algorithm is initialized with
the set of communities C<sub>i−1</sub> found at the previous iteration. This process guarantees that the starting communities are kept, to a certain extent<sup>5</sup>, throughout all the process. As a result of the “moving” threshold, we are able
to study how the structure and the properties of coordinated communities change across the whole spectrum of
coordination. Moreover, the moving threshold implicitly
defines a measure for the extent of coordination observed
at each iteration, that is for each obtained subnetwork.

sources.title: Uncovering Large Groups of Active Malicious Accounts in Online Social Networks
sources.status: Historical Facebook/Instagram production deployment, not current algorithm confirmation
sources.evidence_locator: Introduction; evaluation §8.1 corroborates deployment and precision
sources.why_use: Platform-internal loosely synchronized actions, per-object constraints, Jaccard, scalable group detection.
sources.limits: Private first-party action/IP/target data; precision sampled by security team; no complete recall; favors large active campaigns; no LLM evaluation.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
We have deployed SynchroTrap at Facebook and Instagram for

We have deployed SynchroTrap at Facebook and Instagram for
over ten months (§ 7). In a detailed study of one-month data (§ 8.1),
we observe that it uncovered more than two million malicious accounts and 1156 malicious campaigns. We have randomly sampled
a subset of malicious accounts SynchroTrap caught, and asked security specialists to inspect the accuracy of the results. The manual
inspection suggests that our system achieves a precision higher than
99%.

We evaluate SynchroTrap using a one-month execution log at
Facebook in August 2013.

Second, we
do not invalidate all actions that a malicious account has performed
during a detection window Tp, but conservatively focus on those
that match at least one action of each of the other accounts in the
same cluster. This post processing step helps rule out valid actions
that a user account may have delivered while being compromised.

sources.title: Identifying Correlated Bots in Twitter
sources.status: Real implemented Twitter detector and daily reports at publication; no platform deployment or current service claim
sources.why_use: Cross-account activity correlation and time-warp invariance; exposes dependence beyond account-level scores.
sources.limits: Companion omits full technical algorithm; 94% is approximate-content contextual support via 50 sampled account pairs, not portable population precision; strong timing assumptions.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
We investigate if approximate text matching would increase botness by
employing human judges in Amazon Mechanical Turk. We ask the judges
to determine whether fifty random pairs of accounts are showing similar text
(may not be exact), URLs, authors and languages. We then calculate the
botness. DeBot achieves up to 94 % botness score from the contextual information. Simply put, **94 %** of the tweets are not only synchronized in time,
but also share the same information (Table 1).

We omit technical details of our method,
named DeBot, due to limited presentation scope. The daily reports of bots and
an expanded paper are available in [2].

It is impossible to calculate the exact recall of a bot detection technique because
a complete list of known bots does not exist.

sources.title: Detection of Novel Social Bots by Ensembles of Specialized Classifiers
sources.status: Documented deployed Botometer-v4 service at publication; current availability not checked
sources.why_use: Specialized classifiers plus maximum rule; known-class and unseen-bot evaluation; bridge to operational per-account detection.
sources.limits: Cross-validation AUC is not field precision; scores and datasets shift; v4 != v3 validation study; authors dispute politician ground truth and exclusions.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
In light of these results, we are deploying ESC in the newest version
of Botometer (v4), a tool to detect social bots in the wild that is available through the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe) at Indiana
University. Botometer can be accessed both through an interactive
website (botometer.org) and programmatically through a public
API (rapidapi.com/OSoMe/api/botometer-pro). Fig. 9 illustrates the
system architecture.

Despite impressive results when training and test sets are from

struggle to generalize to novel behaviors.
Despite impressive results when training and test sets are from
the same domain — even using cross-validation — supervised models will miss new classes of bots, leading to low recall.

Another source of bias is that Rauchfleisch and Kaiser [35] overlook
accounts that are no longer available due to suspension, possibly
leading to an underestimation of both precision and recall.

sources.title: The false positive problem of automatic bot detection in social science research
sources.status: Evaluation of Botometer-v3, not universal current-product benchmark
sources.why_use: Base rates, threshold sensitivity, multilingual and temporal validation; safeguards against population prevalence claims.
sources.limits: Five selected datasets, assumed 15% prevalence simulation not measured prevalence; authors and Botometer developers disagree about automated politicians and suspended accounts.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text: A high ROC-AUC score with the original data set and research setting does not translate into a good “precision” for computational social science studies investigating a different context as we show for Botometer v3.

If the numbers of bots are in the minority for the general population (as we assume in this case on Twitter), even a small false-positive rate might lead to a high number of human accounts wrongly classified as bots.

sources.title: Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?
sources.date: 2025-01-17 (v4; first posted 2023-03-17; TMLR publication noted in metadata)
sources.status: Theory plus empirical detector stress tests, not universal impossibility of all provenance
sources.evidence_locator: §4 Hardness of reliable AI text detection
sources.why_use: Distribution-overlap ceiling for text-only detection; experimentally evaluated sensitivity of four detector classes.
sources.limits: Hardness assumption requires human/AI distributions becoming closer; actual text TV difficult to estimate; studied models/passages/attacks not all future detectors.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text: This theorem states that as the TV distance between AI and human text distributions reduces, the AUROC of the best possible detector decreases.

Although the underlying assumption seems to be intuitive given the capabilities of LLMs
such as GPT-4 (OpenAI,2023), a precise analysis of this assumption is quite difficult because estimating the
true TV of the text distributions from a finite set of samples is extremely challenging.
Moreover, retrieval-based detectors are concerning since they might lead to serious privacy issues from storing users’ LLM conversations.

sources.title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers
sources.status: Seven contemporary detectors evaluated on writing samples
sources.evidence_locator: Main text: GPT detectors exhibit bias against non-native English authors
sources.why_use: Concrete subgroup false-positive evidence; warns against linguistic fluency as evidence of bots.
sources.limits: 91 Chinese-forum TOEFL and 88 US eighth-grade essays; not representative platform bot dataset or all later detectors.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text: In our study, we evaluated the performance of seven widely used GPT detectors on 91 TOEFL (Test of English as a Foreign Language) essays from a Chinese forum and 88 US eighth-grade essays from the Hewlett Foundation’s ASAP dataset. While the detectors accurately classified the US student essays, they incorrectly labeled more than half of the TOEFL essays as "AI-generated" (average false-positive rate: 61.3%).

sources.title: New AI classifier for indicating AI-written text
sources.status: Public classifier withdrawn, not current operational detector
sources.why_use: Hard operational status evidence; challenge-set TPR/FPR and short-text/language limits.
sources.limits: Vendor evaluation; historical model; retirement not proof every AI-text detector fails.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text: As of July 20, 2023, the AI classifier is no longer available due to its low rate of accuracy.

In our evaluations on a “challenge set” of English texts, our classifier correctly identifies 26% of AI-written text (true positives) as “likely AI-written,” while incorrectly labeling human-written text as AI-written 9% of the time (false positives).
The classifier is very unreliable on short texts (below 1,000 characters). Even longer texts are sometimes incorrectly labeled by the classifier.

sources.title: A Watermark for Large Language Models
sources.status: Implemented/tested watermark research; this paper does not verify general industry deployment
sources.why_use: Generator-cooperative token watermark with z-test and statistical null; separates provenance marking from blind classifiers.
sources.limits: Requires participating generator and matching scheme/key/tokenizer; entropy/length constraints; limited span-replacement threat model, stronger later stress tests.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
While producing watermarked
text requires access to the language model, detecting the
watermark does not. A third party with knowledge of the
hash function and random number generator can re-produce
the red list for each token and count how many times the red
list rule is violated.

High entropy sequences are detected with
relatively few tokens, while low entropy sequences require
more tokens for detection.

Our analysis assumes the red list is sampled
uniformly at random. This is a deviation from the method
used in practice, which generates red lists using a pseudorandom number generator seeded with previous tokens. The
consequences of pseudo-random sampling are explored in
Section5.

sources.title: Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet
sources.status: Observed real botnet and evaluated detectors; no production detector claim
sources.why_use: Grounded LLM-enabled coordination evidence and striking lab-to-field precision failure.
sources.limits: Single botnet discovered through self-revealing messages; bot/human collection periods differ; not all bot content confirmed AI; thresholds optimized on balanced benchmark.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
Applying
the threshold from earlier (52.7) leads to 815 of the random accounts being labeled
as bots. But these might include many false positives. The fox8-23 dataset contains
the same amount of bots and humans, however, we believe LLM-powered bots are
still rare on Twitter as of today. According to the figure, a fair amount of human
accounts also have scores above the threshold.
Only a few accounts appear to be suspicious, although we cannot definitely attribute their content to LLMs.

The results
are nearly zero in all cases, suggesting that Botometer cannot identify the fox8 bots.

sources.title: Adversarial Creation and Detection of AI-Generated Social Bot Content
sources.status: Implemented/evaluated content classifier; no peer-review or production confirmation in metadata
sources.why_use: New multilingual personalized synthetic-pair training; message→account aggregation improves OOD performance.
sources.limits: Fox8-only in-wild test, older self-revealing bots; two training generators/platforms; text-only; synthetic human-label contamination and topic bias; AUC not calibrated PPV.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text:
Finally, we average the scores of each user’s messages to obtain a user-level score.
The goal is to classify users rather than individual messages, simulating the real-world scenario of detecting AI-powered social bots.
Together, these factors suggest that detection models performing well on this benchmark may struggle significantly against more advanced bots found on today’s platforms.
These models should not be used for automated account bans. Because models can mistakenly identify real people as bots, any punishing action should involve human review.

sources.title: Disrupting malicious uses of AI
sources.date: Undated live official page; retrieved 2026-10-01 (lists 2026 case studies)
sources.why_use: Current operational status anchor: automation plus human investigations, not text-only bot judgments.
sources.limits: Vendor self-report; no public confusion matrix, architecture or globally representative coverage.
sources.read_scope: Main body, methods, results and discussion read; reference lists not treated as evidence.

quotes.text: Automated systems help detect potential violations, while human reviewers play an integral role in identifying and disrupting malicious uses of AI—including scams, malicious cyber activity, covert influence operations, and other harmful or illegal conduct.
Human investigators review activity, connect related cases, and assess behavior in context.

quotes.text: While no one entity has a monopoly on detection, connecting accounts and patterns of behavior has in some cases allowed us to identify previously unreported connections between apparently unrelated sets of activity across platforms.

one account that we banned was used to generate content for both of them. While small in
scale, this suggests a potential previously unreported relationship, at least on the operator
level.
When we analyzed the semantic similarity between the two texts using our models, the analysis concluded that the published version was highly likely a rewrite of the version we identified.
acting on a lead from Meta, we recently banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts whose activity may have been connected to an online scam that appears to have originated in Cambodia.

sources.title: Swarm of micro flying robots in the wild — Zhou et al., Science Robotics 7, eabm5954
sources.type: primary peer-reviewed paper; author-hosted full PDF
sources.why_use: Full-stack decentralized planning architecture; ten-drone bamboo forest and reciprocal-avoidance hardware tests; distinguish four-drone tracking and 40-drone software playground.
sources.limits: Proof-of-concept field experiments, not disaster-response deployment. Broadcast communication assumed; both access-point and peer-to-peer network options. Some automatically extracted plot tables have unlabeled series and are not used as numerical evidence.

quotes.text:
each drone is equipped with full 
perception, localization, planning, and control functionalities and 
loosely coupled by a broadcast network sharing trajectories.

sources.title: Department of Defense Announces Successful Micro-Drone Demonstration — Press Operations NR-008-17, official PACOM mirror
sources.why_use: Named military real-hardware demonstration, date/place and 103-drone scale. Quotes the program director on leaderless collaboration.
sources.limits: Program announcement, not independent evaluation. No telemetry, algorithm, communication protocol or success-rate dataset in release. October 2016 test is not proof of operational battlefield deployment; 1,000 is proposed production batch size.

quotes.text: The test, conducted in October 2016 and documented on Sunday’s CBS News program “60 Minutes”, consisted of 103 Perdix drones launched from three F/A-18 Super Hornets. The micro-drones demonstrated advanced swarm behaviors such as collective decision-making, adaptive formation flying, and self-healing.

sources.title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior — Park et al., arXiv:2304.03442v2 / UIST 2023
sources.type: primary conference research paper; versioned full arXiv HTML
sources.why_use: 25 agents, memory/reflection/planning architecture, central sandbox infrastructure, seeded event coordination and measured information diffusion with memory checks.
sources.limits: Two game days in a constructed world, not organic online society. Researcher-specified identities and initial memories; human crowdworker baseline not maximal human performance. Hallucination, planning errors, high cost; no real-world validation of human social behavior.

quotes.text: During the two-day simulation, the number of agents who knew about Sam’s mayoral candidacy increased from one (4%) to eight (32%), and the number of agents who knew about Isabella’s party increased from one (4%) to thirteen (52%), all without any user intervention.

sources.title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations — Ashery, Aiello and Baronchelli, Science Advances 11(20), eadu9368
sources.type: primary peer-reviewed experimental paper; university repository PDF
sources.why_use: Controlled naming-game experiments distinguish locally incentivized coordination from explicitly designed group goals; baseline 24 agents and tests up to 200; emergent collective bias and convention tipping.
sources.limits: Homogeneous simulated populations and randomly paired letter-choice games, not autonomous communities found online. Finite memory, prompts and payoffs are designed. Unbiased means a statistical test did not detect an initial bias, not proof of exact zero bias. Supplementary Text/data/code not independently re-run.

quotes.text:
A simulation trial consists of a population of *N* interacting agents. 
At each time step, two agents are randomly selected for interaction.

sources.title: Swarm Intelligence: From Natural to Artificial Systems — Bonabeau, Dorigo and Theraulaz (Oxford University Press, 1999), Google Books page-7 excerpt
sources.type: primary book excerpt in bibliographic preview
sources.why_use: Verifiable canonical 1999 definition emphasizing bio-inspired algorithms and distributed problem-solving devices; book excerpt is explicitly attributed to page 7.
sources.limits: Entire book unavailable/read only extracted about-page and displayed page-7 passage; supports this definition, not claims about unviewed chapters.

quotes.text: we extend its definition to include any attempt to design algorithms or distributed problem-solving devices inspired by the collective behavior of social insect colonies and other animal societies.

sources.title: A self-organizing thousand-robot swarm — Harvard SEAS
sources.why_use: Hardware-level infrared communication and locomotion context for Kilobots; institutional corroboration of 1,024 scale.
sources.limits: Institutional publicity, not an independent reproduction. Prefer journal supplement for timings, controls and error limitations; publicity mathematical-guarantee wording should not be generalized to noisy arbitrary hardware.

quotes.text: An infrared transmitter and receiver allow it to communicate with a few of its neighbors and measure their proximity—but the robots are myopic and have no access to a bird’s-eye view.

sources.limits: Gated main text not obtained. Captured full accessible landing-page body, abstract and collateral, not the five-page article. A posted unreviewed critical eLetter is not treated as verified refutation.

sources.title: Supplementary Materials for Programmable self-assembly in a thousand-robot swarm — Rubenstein, Cornejo and Nagpal
sources.type: primary full journal supplementary methods and results PDF
sources.why_use: Full algorithm, four seeds, local distance-gradient/trilateration, 13 trials, counts/timings in Table S1, camera and listening-robot measurement methods, idealized-proof assumptions and real-hardware errors.
sources.limits: Only two 1,024-start trials; remaining repeatability tests much smaller. Approximately twelve-hour assembly on a prepared 2.4 m table. Final shape counts do not equal initial swarm size; removed surplus robots are not necessarily failed robots. Proof assumes idealized conditions. Unlabeled auto-extracted plot numbers not used.

quotes.text:
Both experiments started with 1024 robots and final shapes contained 1018
and 946 robots respectively.

sources.title: Scalable watermarking for identifying large language model outputs — Dathathri et al.
sources.why_use: Generation-time watermark algorithm, actual Gemini deployment, roughly 20-million-response quality study, length/entropy and participation limitations.
sources.limits: Vendor-associated study; not universal generator coverage or campaign detection; current endpoints and released implementation not independently tested.
sources.read_scope: Abstract, main body, evaluation, limitations and methods; supplementary experiments not independently rerun.

quotes.text: We analysed approximately 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked responses and computed the thumbs-up and thumbs-down rates (both as a fraction of the total number of thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback received).
Subsequently, non-distortionary SynthID-Text has been productionized and is currently watermarking responses in Gemini and Gemini Advanced.
In particular, generative watermarks are weakened by edits to the text, such as through LLM paraphrasing
